I dropped 13 of the 20 and replaced them with 13 new ones. I did not run any benchmark data, so the judgments below rest on NAS-Bench-201 domain knowledge.

**Dropped as weak:** The colleague's "could equally be redundant" hypotheses had no clear sign. These were 4/1x1|0/conv3x3, 3/1x1|4/conv3x3, 1/pool|2/conv3x3, 2/1x1|1/conv3x3, 5/1x1|1/pool and 0/conv3x3|4/skip. The sibling "multi-scale" arguments are speculative and unlikely to hold consistently across all three datasets. A few others had a plausible sign but a small margin: 4/3x3|0/3x3, 3/skip|1/conv3x3, 1/pool|2/1x1, 3/pool|4/1x1 and 0/pool|3/none. I kept a few of these in tightened form.

**Kept:**
- Saturation hypotheses: a conv edit helps less when a parallel conv route already exists.
- The edge-3 and edge-4 interactions: removing the direct route makes edge 4 matter more.
- Pooling hypotheses where the mechanism is clear.

**Added:** Connectivity-based interactions are the strongest and most consistent across datasets. An edit on edge 2 is nearly irrelevant if edge 0 or edge 5 is `none`, so its effect is lower. A skip on edge 3 is more valuable when the other routes to the output are removed.
